meta.title: Who really said "The Professor's Lecture Notes Go Straight to the Students' Lecture Notes"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Mark Twain never said it. The earliest documented version is in Harry Lloyd Miller's 1927 book, which credits Edwin E. Slosson. Twain died in 1910.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The Professor's Lecture Notes Go Straight to the Students' Lecture Notes'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Twain — he died in 1910. The joke first appears in print in 1927, credited to chemist and editor Edwin E. Slosson. Here is the paper trail.

answer.label: Not Mark Twain — first credited to Edwin E. Slosson
answer.authorDates: 1865–1929 · American chemist, editor and popular science writer
answer.sourceLine: Mark Twain died in 1910, and Quote Investigator ↗ found “no substantive evidence” connecting the saying to him — the earliest instance it could locate is from 1927, seventeen years after his death. That instance is in Harry Lloyd Miller’s Creative Learning and Teaching, where Miller credits it to “Slosson” — probably Edwin E. Slosson, whose 1910 book Great American Universities makes the same complaint at length. QI is careful to add that no version in Slosson’s own writing has been found, so even his authorship of the polished quip is credited rather than proven.

None documented — not found in his works, and he died in 1910

source.excerpt: In the inimitable phrasing of Slosson, “Lecturing is that mysterious process by means of which the contents of the note-book of the professor are transferred through the instrument of the fountain pen to the note-book of the student without passing through the mind of either.”
trail: 1910 — Edwin E. Slosson gives the argument in full on page 520 of Great American Universities: students who “remove the expressions from their faces,” and an “automatic cut-off” that short-circuits the lecture “from the ear directly to the hand.” Verifiable in the scanned text at the Internet Archive ↗. The idea — but not the epigram.

1927 — the earliest instance Quote Investigator located: Harry Lloyd Miller’s Creative Learning and Teaching, page 120, quoting “the inimitable phrasing of Slosson.” Miller’s book is catalogued at Open Library ↗ as a 1927 Charles Scribner’s Sons title.

1929–1943 — the line comes loose from its author: a Michigan student (1929), Stanford’s Professor Rathburn (1939), and anonymous printings in Mortimer J. Adler’s How to Read a Book (1940) and Evan Esar’s comic dictionary (1943), all catalogued by Quote Investigator ↗.
2012 — the Twain-branded “college is a place” wording appears in a TED blog post on massive online education ↗, the earliest Twain-credited instance QI documents.

source.rightsNote: No copyright status is asserted for the popular Twain-branded wording: it has no identified author and no known first publication, so there is nothing to attach a status to. The two historical texts quoted on this page are a different matter — Slosson’s Great American Universities (Macmillan, 1910) and Miller’s Creative Learning and Teaching (Charles Scribner’s Sons, 1927) were both published well before 1931 and are in the US public domain; the Internet Archive scan of the Slosson is marked not in copyright ↗.

author.name: Edwin E. Slosson
author.kicker: The man it was first credited to
author.heading: About Edwin E. Slosson
author.metaLine: 1865–1929 · American chemist, editor and first head of Science Service
author.bio: Edwin Emery Slosson was an American chemist who became one of the country’s most widely read science popularisers, working as literary editor of The Independent before becoming the first head of Science Service. His 1910 book Great American Universities grew out of a magazine series and was unusually blunt about what he thought lectures actually accomplished. He is better remembered for Creative Chemistry (1919), a genuine bestseller, than for the one-line joke that educators have been crediting to him since 1927.

misattribution.heading: Everyone it has been pinned on
misattribution.intro: This is a saying with an unusually crowded credit line. In the sixteen years after it first appeared in print it was assigned to three different people and left unsigned at least four more times — and Mark Twain, the name attached to it today, is the very last arrival.

items.why: Quote Investigator reports “no substantive evidence connecting this saying to Mark Twain,” and the earliest Twain-credited instance it documents is a TED blog post from June 2012 ↗ about massive online education — more than eighty years after the saying was already in circulation under other names.

A 1939 statistics journal credited him with “A lecture is a process whereby the notes of the professor become the notes of the student without passing through the minds of either,” but QI notes this is a relatively late date ↗ for a saying already in print by 1927.

items.who: An unnamed University of Michigan student
items.why: In March 1929 The American Journal of Nursing printed wording close to Miller’s but ascribed it to “a University of Michigan student” ↗ rather than to Slosson.

National Municipal Review (May 1927), a Texas newspaper and columnist Rex Beach (both 1931), Mortimer J. Adler’s How to Read a Book (1940) and Evan Esar’s comic dictionary (1943) all carried it with no name attached ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The best-supported line of descent runs through Slosson, not Twain: Quote Investigator concludes ↗ that Slosson was the first person to receive credit and the first to write thematically similar passages — while stating plainly that there is “no direct evidence yet that he wrote one of the clever and concise versions of the quip.”

context.heading: Why the joke had teeth
lead: Slosson was not making a joke in 1910 — he was making an accusation. In the closing pages of Great American Universities he described a lecture hall as “about as inspiring an audience as a roomful of phonographs holding up their brass trumpets,” and claimed students had unconsciously wired themselves an “automatic cut-off” that ran the lecture from ear to hand without troubling the brain in between.

Somebody — possibly Slosson, possibly a colleague quoting him loosely — compressed that page of invective into one sentence, and the sentence has outlived the argument by a century. It was reprinted anonymously through the 1930s and 40s, ascribed to a Stanford professor in 1939 and to an unnamed Michigan student in 1929, and only picked up Mark Twain’s name once online education gave it a second life.
context.detailsSummary: The full chain of attributions, 1910 to 2012
detailsBody: 1910 — Slosson’s Great American Universities, page 520: the phonograph passage and the “automatic cut-off” that short-circuits the lecture “from the ear directly to the hand.” The idea, but not the epigram.
1927 — Miller’s Creative Learning and Teaching gives the fountain-pen version and credits Slosson; the same year, National Municipal Review gives a plainer version and credits only “some cynic.”

1928–1943 — Edward Randall Maguire repeats Miller’s Slosson credit; the American Journal of Nursing hands it to a Michigan student; Texas newspapers and columnist Rex Beach run it unsigned; a statistics journal gives it to Stanford’s Professor Rathburn; Mortimer J. Adler and Evan Esar both print it anonymously.
2012 — a TED blog post on massive online education opens with “Mark Twain thought so,” and the Twain version is the one that now circulates.

schema.verdictNote: Commonly misattributed to Mark Twain, who died in 1910. The earliest documented instance (1927) credits Edwin E. Slosson, but Quote Investigator found no version in Slosson’s own writing, so his authorship is credited rather than established.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator states there is no substantive evidence connecting the saying to Mark Twain; the earliest citation it located is Harry Lloyd Miller's 1927 book Creative Learning and Teaching (p. 120), which credits 'Slosson'; QI concludes Edwin E. Slosson was the first to receive credit but there is no direct evidence he wrote the concise quip. The page also documents the May 1927 National Municipal Review 'some cynic' version, 1928 Maguire, March 1929 American Journal of Nursing ('a University of Michigan student'), January and April 1931 anonymous newspaper versions, 1939 Professor Rathburn of Stanford in a statistics journal, 1940 Mortimer J. Adler's How to Read a Book, 1943 Evan Esar, and a 26 June 2012 TED blog post crediting Mark Twain.
Great American Universities by Edwin Emery Slosson (1865-1929) was published in 1910 by Macmillan, New York, and the Internet Archive scan is freely readable and marked NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT.

Page 520 of Great American Universities contains the passages about students who 'remove the expressions from their faces', the 'roomful of phonographs holding up their brass trumpets', and the 'automatic cut-off which goes into operation as they open their notebooks and short-circuits the train of thought from the ear directly to the hand'.

Edwin Emery Slosson lived 7 June 1865 to 15 October 1929, was an American chemist, editor and science populariser, literary editor of The Independent and the first head of Science Service, and wrote Great American Universities (1910) and Creative Chemistry (1919).
Mark Twain (Samuel Langhorne Clemens), American writer and humorist, was born 30 November 1835 and died 21 April 1910.
Creative Learning and Teaching by Harry Lloyd Miller was published in 1927 by C. Scribner's Sons.

The Center for Mark Twain Studies runs an ongoing series, 'The Apocryphal Twain', documenting quotations commonly and falsely attributed to Mark Twain; it does not include an entry on the lecture-notes quotation.
